summary:
Borno stands under the national framework: Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), which also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, public shows of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and which Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records police using to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Borno is one of the twelve northern states that had adopted Sharia into its criminal legislation by 2002, with Sharia courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law (Human Rights Watch, 2004). The UK Home Office note (June 2025) confirms that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states, criminalising same-sex acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for sodomy for men is death in all twelve states, and penalties for lesbianism range from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note includes a dedicated section on enforcement of Sharia provisions and the attitude of the hisbah, the morality police.

Borno's own statute deepens the exposure. Borno State's law on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities (2000), gazetted in Borno State Gazette No. 42 Vol. 26 on 18 October 2001 and signed by Governor Kachalla on 10 December 2000, makes engaging in prostitution, lesbianism, a homosexual act or pimping an offence in the state (Section 3); Section 7 provides that any person who engages in sexual intercourse with another person of the same gender shall upon conviction be punished with death; Section 4 deems all brothels closed on commencement; and Section 9 assigns jurisdiction to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts. The death penalty enacted in Borno's own statute means the state's criminalisation of same-sex conduct rests on Borno legislation as well as the federal framework.

Borno separately enacted its own Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 3 March 2003, with no operation date or gazette identified in the sourcebook. The Borno text was obtained only in May 2006, after the volume's annotation had been completed, which is why Borno is not among the individually annotated codes. The parallel Sharia layer for Borno therefore rests on a Borno-specific enactment rather than on federal or umbrella coverage.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.
tangentialFactors:
Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case surfaced in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, which she served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
